answer:
RECOMMENDATION: the second option. Record the frozen extract as a new entity brought into
existence by an event that also diminished the moth - not as a part carried under the specimen's
existing identity. And no, that choice is not what makes the extract "from the paratype": the
paratype link is carried by events, and it is stronger, not weaker, for keeping the two identities
apart.

1. WHY OPTION 1 IS NOT AVAILABLE IN THE MODEL

In the CRM a part and its whole are always two individuals. E80 Part Removal is quantified as
necessarily carrying both P112 diminished (the thing made smaller) and P113 removed (the thing
taken away), each ranging over E18 Physical Thing - the construct presupposes two instances, not
one identity wearing two catalogue numbers. Nothing lets one E18's identifier stand for a detached
piece: P1 is identified by / P48 has preferred identifier attach an E42 Identifier to one entity.
If you gave the extract the moth's identity you would be asserting that the extract IS the moth,
and you would then be unable to state the thing you actually want to state - that it CAME FROM the
moth.

The SIG has already settled the surrounding question. Issue 574 (thread t1536) relaxed the range of
P112 diminished from E24 Physical Human-Made Thing to E18 Physical Thing precisely so that cutting
parts from natural objects could be recorded; Martin Doerr's summary of the earlier debate there is
the governing principle - the SIG had considered whether a natural object becomes "human made" the
instant a part is broken off it for sampling and decided that this violates identity criteria of
classes: "It just leaves a human-made feature on a natural object." Clipping the leg therefore
changes neither the moth's class nor its identity. It stays one E20 Biological Object, diminished,
with its original E42 Identifier.

2. WHAT TO RECORD

The clipping - one event, two co-instantiated classes. This is not a choice between the sampling
view and the modification view: CRMsci declares S2 Sample Taking and E80 Part Removal as the two
subclasses of S1 Matter Removal, and declares P112 diminished a subproperty of O1 diminished, so
the two views compose.

  S2 Sample Taking + E80 Part Removal
    O3 sampled from / P112 diminished -> the pinned moth (E20 Biological Object). CRMsci declares
      E18 Physical Thing a subclass of S10 Material Substantial, so an E20 is a legitimate range
      for O3 and O1.
    O4 sampled at -> E53 Place, the spot on the specimen the leg came from
    O5 removed / P113 removed -> the leg (S13 Sample; also E20, being matter from an organism)
    P14 carried out by -> the graduate student; P4 has time-span -> last year
  Both P112/P113 and P14/P4 are quantified as necessary on their domains, so record them.

The extraction - the leg ceases, the extract begins:

  E81 Transformation + E12 Production
    P124 transformed -> the leg
    P123 resulted in / P108 has produced -> the extract
  This is the pairing the CRM itself asks for. E12 Production's scope note says an event should
  also be documented as an E81 Transformation if it destroys objects and simultaneously produces
  others from their parts or material, and that in this case the new items have separate
  identities: matter is preserved, identity is not. E80's scope note points the same way (part
  removal plus production, where the removed matter has no discernible identity before removal but
  does after), and S1 Matter Removal's scope note says such cases "should be modelled by using
  multiple instantiation with adequate concepts of creating the respective items".
  If you would rather not type a tube of eluate as an E24 Physical Human-Made Thing, drop P108 and
  P123 and use the E63/E64 halves of E81 instead: P92 brought into existence -> the extract, P93
  took out of existence -> the leg. Both range on E77 Persistent Item, and S13 Sample accepts them.

  The extract: S13 Sample - taken from an S10 Material Substantial with the intention of being
  representative of some of its material qualities - optionally also S12 Amount of Fluid for its
  physical form, with its own new E42 Identifier via P1 is identified by / P48 has preferred
  identifier.

  Useful shortcut alongside the events: the moth O25 contains the extract. O25 was written for
  exactly this situation - containment "regardless of whether the identity of the involved
  instances is based on the persistence of the form of material or on material substance that may
  change form" - and it generalises P46 is composed of. It survives the dissolution of the leg,
  which P46 would not.

If your records genuinely never treated the leg as a thing, you may collapse the two events into a
single S2 Sample Taking + E80 Part Removal + E12 Production whose O5 removed is the extract. The
cost is that you lose the fact that what left the moth was a leg rather than an aliquot of DNA. I
would keep the two events, linked by the leg.

3. THE PARATYPE

Being a paratype is not a material property, so it cannot travel with matter. In the CRM it is a
relation between the specimen and the taxon. The 1932 description is an E83 Type Creation - whose
scope note names this case explicitly, noting that in the life sciences the type is a "taxon", the
type description a "protologue" and the exemplary specimens "original element" or "holotype" - with
P135 created type -> the species as an E55 Type, and P136 was based on -> the pinned moth,
qualified by its taxonomic role ("paratype"; P136's FOL declares the ternary role form). The
standing statement about the specimen is P137 exemplifies -> the species, using P137.1 in the
taxonomic role; P137's own example is a natural-history one, a Clayton Herbarium object (E20)
exemplifying a species in the taxonomic role lectotype. Christian-Emil Ore's remark in t0375 -
"P137 was introduced to deal with type specimens in natural history" - is where that construct
comes from.

So the answer to the second half is: the identity choice does not affect it, because "from the
paratype" is a provenance claim, not an identity claim. What makes it true is a recorded chain from
the extract back to the entity that bears the P136/P137 taxonomic role - S2 Sample Taking O3
sampled from the moth, O5 removed the leg, E81 Transformation from the leg to the extract, with
O25 containment as the queryable shortcut. Option 1 would not strengthen that claim, it would
dissolve it: an extract that IS the paratype cannot be FROM the paratype, and you would also lose
the ability to say that the paratype is intact in its drawer while a derivative sits at -80C.

Do not attach P136 or P137 to the extract. The extract is not an exemplary specimen of the taxon;
it is evidence derived from one. Martin Doerr's framing of split samples in t1080 is the right one:
once a unit of matter is taken it makes its own history, but the "sampleness" goes back to the
initial removal. The extract has its own number, store, keeper and condition history; what it
inherits from the moth is derivation, not identity.

One trap to avoid: do not reach for S24 Sample Splitting with O27 split / O29 removed sub-sample
for the leg-to-extract step, even though it looks like sub-sampling. O29's scope note requires that
the sub-sample "maintains the characteristic qualities of the original", and a chemical extract of
one molecule class does not. That construct is for homogeneous division (see t1261, where fibres
are split off a paper sample); dissolving a leg into a DNA extract is a transformation, not a
split.

rejected_alternatives.option: Carrying the extract under the specimen's existing identity (option 1 in the question): the moth's E42 Identifier / P1 is identified by reused for the extract
rejected_alternatives.why_not: E80 Part Removal necessarily has both P112 diminished and P113 removed, each ranging on E18 Physical Thing, so the construct already presupposes two individuals; and an E42 Identifier is attached to one entity. Reusing the number asserts the extract is the moth, which makes the statement you actually want - that it came from the moth - unsayable, and hides that the two now have divergent locations, keepers and condition histories.

rejected_alternatives.option: P46 is composed of, to keep the extract as a part of the moth
rejected_alternatives.why_not: P46 relates two instances of E18 Physical Thing whose identity rests on stability of form, and the extract is neither part of the moth any more nor a form-stable thing. CRMsci's O25 contains, of which P46 is a subproperty, is the form-independent generalisation and covers matter that 'was or is contained' in another material substantial even when its form changes.

rejected_alternatives.option: S24 Sample Splitting with O27 split / O29 removed sub-sample for the leg-to-extract step
rejected_alternatives.why_not: O29's scope note requires the resulting sub-sample to maintain the characteristic qualities of the original sample. A DNA extract does not maintain the leg's qualities; it isolates one component. Splitting is for homogeneous division (t1261's fibres off a paper sample).

rejected_alternatives.option: S3 Measurement by Sampling for the whole episode
rejected_alternatives.why_not: S3 covers sampling and analysis as one unit of activity where the sample is typically not identified or preserved beyond the activity. Here the sample is catalogued and kept at -80C, which is exactly the case S3's scope note excludes.

rejected_alternatives.option: E17 Type Assignment classifying the moth as 'paratype'
rejected_alternatives.why_not: It would record a classification of the moth on its own and lose which taxon it is a paratype of. The CRM supplies the taxonomic-role qualifier on P136 was based on and P137 exemplifies precisely because paratype is a role in a relation between a specimen and a taxon, not a property of the specimen alone.

rejected_alternatives.option: Staying in CRMbase only (E80 Part Removal + E12 Production, no CRMsci)
rejected_alternatives.why_not: CRMbase alone cannot say that the matter was taken to be representative of the specimen (S13 Sample / O3 sampled from), cannot record where on the specimen it was taken (O4 sampled at), and has no form-independent containment (O25) to survive the leg's dissolution. This is a sampling case, so use CRMsci; it is a proper extension of CRMbase, and E80 is declared a subclass of S1 Matter Removal there, so nothing is lost.

siblings_considered.why_not: A pinned, mounted specimen is a human preparation, so E22 Human-Made Object is tempting. But the SIG's conclusion in issue 574 / t1536 is that human intervention on a natural object does not make the object human-made - it 'just leaves a human-made feature on a natural object'. E20's scope note allows co-instantiating E22 for artificial assemblages such as Victorian butterfly frames, i.e. for the mount, but the moth that was clipped stays an E20 with its identity unchanged.

E80 Part Removal is S2's only sibling under S1 Matter Removal, and it is not a rival I can reject - it is the other aspect of the same event, which is why I co-instantiate both. Used alone it cannot express that the matter was taken to be representative of the specimen (O3 sampled from / O5 removed to an S13 Sample) nor where on the specimen it was taken (O4 sampled at).

E80's own scope note pairs it with E12 Production when the removed part had no discernible identity before removal but has one after, so a reader will ask why the clipping is not also a Production. Because the leg never acquired a documented identity - it was consumed. The identity is acquired by the extract, which is created by the later extraction event, so that is where E12 belongs.

E65 Creation is for conceptual and immaterial products. The DNA extract is matter in a tube, not a proposition. (The barcode sequence eventually derived from it would be the E65 side of this story, but that is a later, separate event.)

E6 Destruction would record that the leg lost its identity but leave the extract's origin unstated. E81 Transformation, being both E63 Beginning of Existence and E64 End of Existence, records the destruction and the causally connected creation as one event, which is what 'dissolved into an extract' is.

S12 Amount of Fluid says only that the thing is a confined liquid; it carries none of the sampled-from semantics that make the extract traceable to the specimen. It can be co-instantiated for the physical form, but S13 Sample is what does the work here.

No sibling of E42 is a plausible rival - a museum catalogue number is an identifier, not a title, a time primitive or a space primitive. E35 Title is the closest of them and I name it only because the rule asks.

E89 Propositional Object is a real rival here: in t0375 Christian-Emil Ore observed that a species can be regarded as a hypothetical set expressible by a logical proposition, which pulls the taxon towards E89. But the CRM's own construct for taxa is E55 - E83 Type Creation's scope note calls the created type a taxon, and P135 created type, P136 was based on and P137 exemplifies with their taxonomic-role qualifiers only work against E55.

notes: Three tool frictions. (1) The hierarchy is indexed asymmetrically across models: S10 Material Substantial's dossier says it is the superclass of E18, but E18's own dossier shows only 'Subclass of: E72', so `connect S2 E20` and `connect S2 E18` do not offer O3 sampled from or O1 diminished even though CRMsci declares them applicable to any E18. I had to read the relationship off S10's dossier. Anyone using `connect` alone would conclude, wrongly, that a museum specimen cannot be the source of an S2 Sample Taking. (2) `concept S24` returns 'No such concept' although O27 split and O29 removed sub-sample are declared with S24 Sample Splitting as their domain; I reconstructed S24 from those two property dossiers plus the 50th-meeting minutes surfaced by `docs --kind minutes`. (3) Class and property scope notes are not addressable as quotable chunk ids (`quote E12`, `quote decl:E12` etc. all return UNKNOWN SOURCE), so the E12/E80/S1/S13/O25/O29 scope-note wording I rely on is paraphrased or given as short fragments read verbatim from `concept` output rather than cited with the {id, quote} form. E83 Type Creation is exempt from siblings_considered: the tool reports it is the only subclass of E65. Residual uncertainty, which is why one detail is hedged in the answer rather than asserted: whether a tube of DNA eluate should be typed E24 Physical Human-Made Thing (letting P108 has produced and P123 resulted in apply) or kept strictly as S11/S13 amount of matter (forcing the P92/P93 route). I found no SIG decision on that boundary for laboratory extracts; the closest material is the S11 identity discussion in t1080, which settles that form stability is not required of a sample but does not settle the E18/S11 typing of a preparation.
